compiler_note: Source index of public reporting and judgments. It is not a manual, not an expression of support for any proscribed organisation, and not a complete police schedule. Palestine Action has been described by police as linked to several hundred actions; this file covers the actions that became named cases or that CAGE documented, plus the public-law case about the ban.
how_to_use: Each object is one case or one clearly bounded series. Filter on category, nickname, or action_dates. independent_source_count excludes the CAGE dossier itself. Damage figures are copied from the outlet that stated them and often disagree.

legal_status_of_the_ban.status_on_compile_date: Proscription in force. The Court of Appeal allowed the Home Secretary's appeal and set aside the quashing order.

primary_dossier.title: Putting Bodies on the Line: The Landscape of Direct Action and Civil Disobedience for Palestine in Britain
primary_dossier.disclaimer_printed_in_the_pdf: Nothing in this report should be understood as support or as an expression of support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

limits: Ten independent sources was realistic for Filton, the proscription case, Brize Norton, Defend Our Juries, Barclays, Allianz, the Balfour statue and Oldham. It was not realistic for a one-day lock-on that only two outlets covered. Those cases are still included, with the sources that exist.
No BAILII transcript of the Filton or Teledyne criminal sentences was found. Those outcomes rest on contemporaneous court reporting.
Defendant lists for the wider Filton 24 are incomplete. Only names read in opened reports are included.
A few URLs come from the CAGE bibliography after PDF text extraction. The Mancunian Matters URL was line-broken in the PDF and is omitted rather than guessed.
Social posts are included only where the post itself is a report with a link, not as evidence of the underlying fact.

cases.location: Multiple Elbit-linked sites, including London HQ and UAV Engines, Shenstone
cases.target: Elbit Systems UK and related sites
cases.charges: Bundle of criminal damage, burglary, threatening to damage property, possessing articles, and encouraging criminal damage, covering several 2020-21 actions. Not every defendant was on every count.

outcome.result: Jury returned 12 not-guilty verdicts. Richard Barnard convicted of one count of criminal damage and given a conditional discharge. Jury hung on 23 other counts. Six defendants (Barnard, Ammori, Scherer, Cooney, Brouard, Arnott), later called the Elbit Six, were listed for a retrial, reported as listed into 2027. Declassified UK later reported Elbit lobbied the Home Office for that retrial.

cases.summary: First major consolidated Palestine Action prosecution. Trial opened 13 November 2023. Defendants rejected a plea deal under which Ammori and Barnard would plead guilty and the others would be acquitted. Prosecution witness Ofer Meishar, Elbit chief security officer, did not attend; the report says an Israeli government letter said he could not leave Israel.

cases.location: Elbit Systems UK, Aztec West, Filton, near Bristol

defendants.note: Reporting uses Filton 6, Filton 18, Filton 24 and Filton 25 for overlapping groups. Twenty-four people were charged in connection with the 6 August 2024 action. Not every name of the wider 24 was confirmed from a primary court list in this pass.

cases.court: Woolwich Crown Court, Mr Justice Jeremy Johnson (first six); second group at the Old Bailey before Judge Patrick Field KC; a retrial listing was later mentioned at Manchester Crown Court
cases.charges: Aggravated burglary, criminal damage, violent disorder. Samuel Corner also faced GBH with intent. CPS did not charge a terrorism offence but asked the judge to treat the offending as having a terrorism connection under s.69 Sentencing Act 2020.

outcome.first_trial_verdicts: 2026-02-04. All six not guilty of aggravated burglary. Rajwani, Rogers and Devlin not guilty of violent disorder. No verdict on criminal damage, or on Corner's GBH count, or on violent disorder for the other three.
outcome.rest_of_24: 2026-02-18. Al Jazeera reported the remaining defendants were formally acquitted of aggravated burglary after the prosecution offered no evidence.
outcome.retrial: 2026-05-05, Woolwich. Head, Corner, Kamio and Rajwani guilty of criminal damage. Rogers and Devlin not guilty. Corner not guilty of GBH with intent; guilty by 11-1 of GBH without intent.

sentences_2026-06-12.Charlotte Head: 6 years less 45 days, plus a driving disqualification
sentences_2026-06-12.Samuel Corner: 8 years 8 months, covering criminal damage and GBH without intent

outcome.terrorism_connection: Johnson ruled the criminal-damage offences had a terrorist connection. Reporting describes this as the first time a UK criminal-damage conviction was sentenced with that enhancement. The finding was not a count on the indictment and was not left to the jury.
outcome.second_trial: From 22 June 2026, eight alleged organisers. Wikipedia and later reporting: jury acquitted William Plastow of violent disorder; after 37 hours, Sean Middlebrough guilty of criminal damage; no verdict on seven others. A retrial was provisionally listed, with dates reported as June 2027 or June 2028 depending on the outlet. Treat the relisting date as unsettled.
outcome.contempt: Contempt proceedings were opened against defence barrister Rajiv Menon KC over his first-trial closing speech. Jurisdiction was disputed; a substantive hearing was adjourned.
outcome.site: Elbit later closed the Aztec West site. September 2025 is the date given on the Wikipedia page.

cases.summary: On 6 August 2024 people entered the Filton Elbit site. Prosecutors said damage was about £1 million to £1.2 million, and that a police officer, named in Wikipedia as Kate Evans, suffered a spinal fracture. The six people accused of being inside were held on remand for about 17 months before the first trial, which ran from 17 November 2025. The judge refused a necessity/Gaza defence. Five of the six were bailed after the February acquittals on aggravated burglary; Corner was not. At the retrial the judge restricted what the defence could tell the jury. Sentences in June 2026 totalled a little over 26 years before the 45-day deductions.

cases.location: High Court and Court of Appeal, London
cases.target: The Home Secretary's decision to proscribe Palestine Action
defendants: Claimant: Huda Ammori. Defendant: Secretary of State for the Home Department.
cases.court: King's Bench Divisional Court and Court of Appeal (Civil Division)
cases.charges: Not a criminal case. Judicial review of an order under section 3 Terrorism Act 2000 adding Palestine Action to Schedule 2.

outcome.order: Decision taken 20 June 2025. Order made 4 July 2025, in force 5 July 2025. Commons vote reported as 385 to 26.
outcome.permission: [2025] EWHC 1708 (Admin), Chamberlain J, and [2025] EWCA Civ 1311 (17 October 2025) on permission / interim issues. A further permission judgment is cited as [2025] EWHC 2013 (Admin).
outcome.divisional_court: [2026] EWHC 292 (Admin), 13 February 2026, Dame Victoria Sharp PQBD, Swift J and Steyn J. Proscription quashed as contrary to the Home Secretary's own policy and disproportionate under Articles 10 and 11 ECHR.
outcome.court_of_appeal: [2026] EWCA Civ 721, 15 June 2026. Home Secretary's appeal allowed on both grounds. Quashing order set aside. Proscription held lawful. Cross-appeal on procedural fairness and Article 14 refused. A Scottish petition, Murray v Advocate General (COS-P1017-25), was noted as ongoing.

cases.summary: The legal status of the ban changed twice in 2026. From 13 February to 15 June the High Court quashing stood. From 15 June the Court of Appeal reinstated the ban. Support, membership and uniform offences under sections 11 to 13 Terrorism Act 2000 attach again. Maximum on indictment for sections 11 and 12 is 14 years.

cases.location: Parliament Square and nationwide, including Norwich and the Labour conference in Liverpool
cases.target: The proscription itself. The act alleged is displaying a sign reading 'I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.'
defendants: Early named defendants include Jeremy Shippam, Judit Murray, and later Tim Crosland, David Nixon, Dawn Manners, Gwen Harrison, Melanie Griffith and Patrick Friend. Muhammad Rabbani of CAGE was arrested on 4 October 2025. Most of the hundreds arrested are not named in open reporting.
cases.court: Magistrates' courts. Charges under sections 12 and 13 Terrorism Act 2000, authorised in batches by postal charge requisition.
cases.charges: Inviting support, or displaying an article in a public place in such a way as to arouse reasonable suspicion of membership or support.

outcome.result: Arrest totals, which differ by outlet and by the hour they were counted: 29 on 5 July 2025 in Parliament Square, three later charged; 70+ on 12 July; 100+ on 19 July including 55 in Parliament Square; Met said 474 on 9 August, later revised by the BBC to 532 of which 521 were for the placard; more than 425 on 6 September; 66 in Liverpool on 29 September including an 83-year-old; a further mass vigil on 4 October. First three defendants pleaded not guilty on 16 September 2025. CPS said on 5 September 2025 that charged cases had reached 138, plus 24 more. These numbers moved quickly and should be re-checked against CPS releases.

cases.summary: After proscription, Defend Our Juries organised open sign-holding. The criminal allegation is the sign, not property damage. Banksy's Royal Courts mural of 8 September 2025 is a related news event, not a prosecution.

cases.target: Ministerial contact with Elbit and Israeli officials about protests

outcome.result: Not a criminal case. FOI material and the ministerial meetings register show Priti Patel met Elbit on 2 March 2022 to discuss protests and security; Chris Philp met Elbit, police and an AGO representative on 19 April 2023; the Guardian reported in August 2023 that Israeli embassy officials tried to influence UK prosecutions. Declassified UK's June 2025 piece is the Elbit letter asking for the Elbit Eight retrial.
